scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Pendet originated as a floral offering ritual dance performed in Balinese Hindu temples to welcome gods descending from khayangan.
It was initially part of piodalan ceremonies and symbolized gratitude and respect.
In the 1950s, I Wayan Rindi and Ni Ketut Reneng codified the dance with four dancers for tourism shows in Denpasar.
on_screen: Map: Indonesia · Southeast Asia
Image 1 with attribution

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Pendet is performed during temple ceremonies (piodalan), social events, and tourism shows.
It symbolizes welcoming gods, spirits, and guests, expressing gratitude, respect, and joy.
The dance is a form of Bebalihan (entertainment dance) rather than a sacred Wali dance.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Pendet is performed by 4-5 young girls carrying small silver bowls decorated with young palm leaves, filled with flower petals and incense.
The dancers move from shrine to shrine within temple yards, sprinkling petals to welcome gods and guests.
Movements are simple, foundational Balinese dance steps learned by imitation, suitable for beginners.
Watch for Petal Sprinkle.

scenes.title: The people
narration: I Wayan Rindi and Ni Ketut Reneng codified the dance in the 1950s.
I Wayan Beratha expanded the choreography and scale in the 1960s, including the mass performance at the 1962 Asian Games.
Pendet is a Balinese dance and part of Indonesian traditional dance forms, classified as Bebalihan (entertainment dance) distinct from sacred Wali dances.
